# Clustering with kmeans() and hclust()

We will begin by making up some data to cluster. 

```{r}
tmp <- c(rnorm(30, 3), rnorm(30, -3))
x <- cbind(x = tmp, y = rev(tmp))
plot(x)
```
## Run kmeans()

```{r}
k <- kmeans(x, centers = 2, nstart=20)
k
```
> Q. What size is each cluster? 

```{r}
k$size
```

> Q. Cluster centers

```{r}
k$centers
```

>Q. Membership Vector

```{r}
k$cluster
```

Plot our data with the clustering result

```{r}
plot(x, col=k$cluster)
points(k$centers, col="blue", pch=16, cex=2)
```


## hclust()

Hierarchical Clustering
```{r}
hc <- hclust( dist(x) )
hc
```

There is a cool and useful plot method for hclust()

```{r}
plot(hc)
```
#Principal Component Analysis 

First we will look at data from the UK and look at the foods they eat and drink. 

First read the data from online. 
```{r}
url <- "https://tinyurl.com/UK-foods"
x <- read.csv(url, row.names=1)
x
```

Let's make some typical plots 

```{r}
mycols <- rainbow(nrow(x))
barplot( as.matrix(x), col=mycols)
```

Make it side by side i.e. not sstacked 

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), col = mycols, beside = T)
```

One plot that is helpful here.

```{r}
pairs(x, col=mycols)
```

# PCA!

Do PCA of this 17D UK food data. The main function in base R is called `prcomp()`.
This function wants the inverse of this data so the countries in the rows and the foods in the columns.

```{r}
pca <- prcomp(t(x))
summary(pca)
```

The `prcomp()` function returns a list object. 

```{r}
plot(pca)
```

The "PCA plot" a.k.a a PCA score plot is a plot of PC1 vs PC2. Basically using the new PCA axis to view our data. 

```{r}
attributes(pca)
```
We will focus on `pca$x` for this plot

```{r}
pca$x
```

```{r}
plot(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,2], xlab="PC1", ylab = "PC2")
text(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,2], labels = colnames(x))
```

> Q7. Complete the code below to generate a plot of PC1 vs PC2. The second line adds text labels over the data points.

```{r}

library(ggplot2)
# Create a data frame for plotting
df <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
df$Country <- rownames(df)

# Plot PC1 vs PC2 with ggplot
ggplot(pca$x) +
  aes(PC1, PC2, label = rownames(pca$x)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5) +
  xlim(-270, 500) +
  xlab("PC1") +
  ylab("PC2") +
  theme_bw()
```
> Q8. Customize your plot so that the colors of the country names match the colors in our UK and Ireland map and table at start of this document.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
# Create a data frame for plotting
df <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
df$Country <- rownames(df)

# Plot PC1 vs PC2 with ggplot
ggplot(df) +
  aes(x = PC1, PC2, label = Country, color = Country) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5) +
  xlim(-270, 500) +
  xlab("PC1") +
  ylab("PC2") +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "yellow", "blue", "green"))
```
> Q9: Generate a similar ‘loadings plot’ for PC2. What two food groups feature prominantely and what does PC2 mainly tell us about?

### What this type of plot for PC2 is what specific types of food drive the separation for this principal component. So Scotland sits where it does in principal component 2 because they consume way more soft drinks than other countries, and also less fresh potatoes than Wales which has the highest levels of fresh potato consumption. This principal component is mostly driven by soft drink and fresh potato consumption. 


```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(x = PC2, 
      y = reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC2)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  xlab("PC2 Loading Score") +
  ylab("") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```

## PCA of a RNA-seq 

```{r}
url2 <- "https://tinyurl.com/expression-CSV"
rna.data <- read.csv(url2, row.names=1)
head(rna.data)
```

```{r}
pcaRNA <- prcomp(t(rna.data))
summary(pcaRNA)
```
Make our PCA score
```{r}
plot(pcaRNA$x[,1], pcaRNA$x[,2])
text(pcaRNA$x[,1], pcaRNA$x[,2], labels = colnames(rna.data))
```
